edges.relationship: Wrigley uses de Vries’s urbanization research and the joint work of de Vries and van der Woude to compare English growth with earlier Dutch development.
edges.evidence_note: Own Quest (2003), 152–155, notes 12–23, uses European Urbanization (1984) and the JOINT de Vries/van der Woude First Modern Economy (1997) to compare urban growth, occupations, productivity and incomes. Van der Woude retains equal credit. Bairoch, Batou and Chèvre supply a separate 1988 dataset with a different geographical scope (note 13); the calculations are not all de Vries’s alone. This is an empirical and comparative resource, not formal mentorship or independent verification of every figure. The Smithian limits discussed at 157 do not automatically constitute criticism of de Vries.

edges.relationship: Wrigley uses Mokyr’s two-sector calculation to illustrate why rapid growth in a small modern sector need not produce an immediate surge in aggregate growth.
edges.evidence_note: Own Quest (2003), 167–168, note 50, explicitly credits Mokyr’s authored editor’s introduction (1993), page 12, in his edited British Industrial Revolution. Wrigley uses the calculation for a somewhat similar purpose: hypothetical modern and traditional sectors initially comprise 10 and 90 percent and grow at 4 and 1 percent; they become equal after 74 years, with aggregate growth then 2.5 percent. This is an illustrative model, not an observed historical estimate, adoption of an entire school, or a fresh reading of Mokyr’s chapter. No independent numerical replication is claimed.

edges.relationship: Genovese draws on Woodward’s account of intertwined Black and Southern cultures and credits his indispensable advice and criticism.
edges.evidence_note: Own Roll, Jordan, Roll preface quotes Woodward’s American Counterpoint on mutually shaped Black and Southern cultures; the acknowledgments call his encouragement, advice and criticism indispensable. This is a specific intellectual framing and critical resource, not certification of Genovese’s nationality thesis, formal mentorship, or a fresh reading of Woodward’s whole book. Later criticism of Genovese’s paternalism remains intact.

edges.relationship: Genovese credits Davis with sharing ideas and helping revise Roll, Jordan, Roll section by section.
edges.evidence_note: The acknowledgments describe Davis, concurrently resident at Stanford, reading the manuscript section by section, sharing ideas and helping over rough spots while writing his own book. This supports a substantive intellectual and revision contribution, not coauthorship or agreement with every conclusion. Existing reverse Genovese→Davis resource edge_1866 and Davis→Genovese political critique edge_1867 remain unchanged.

edges.relationship: Genovese gives qualified support to Du Bois’s claim that exploitation intensified in slavery’s final decade.
edges.evidence_note: Own Farmers, Planters, and Overseers, paragraph beginning Contrary to legend, gives SOME credence to Du Bois’s exploitation claim in light of a dip in reproduction rates, immediately qualifying this with if so and denying overseers full or primary responsibility. This records Genovese’s particular argumentative use, not independently verified demography or wholesale endorsement of Du Bois. The permitted public preview is unpaginated; adjacent notes 34–35 do not expose the terminal reference. No exact Du Bois work is inferred from the separate Black Reconstruction permissions list.

edges.relationship: Chatterjee calls the Communist Manifesto a persistently powerful formative book and locates himself within Marxist scholarly currents.
edges.evidence_note: Direct 2011 Q4–Q5 testimony concerns the jointly authored Marx–Engels Manifesto. Engels has no full endpoint, but shared authorship remains explicit. No edition, translation, first encounter date, direct teacher, or acceptance of every Marxist theory is claimed.

edges.relationship: Repeated reading of Gramsci helped Chatterjee rethink civil and political society, alongside the collective’s earlier subaltern-class starting point.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2011 Q1 credits repeated Gramsci readings for the initial idea of disjuncture, while saying Gramsci does not formulate it in those words. Chatterjee’s analysis of Indian democracy in the 1990s and later self-criticism remain his own. The McGrail interview describes collective English Prison Notebooks reading, not exclusive discovery or a verified account of terminology and censorship. No exact English edition, translators or original notebooks were newly checked.

edges.relationship: Chatterjee names Guha’s Prose of Counterinsurgency as a particularly effective exemplar of reading elite archives against the grain.
edges.evidence_note: In the McGrail interview Chatterjee includes himself in the collective effort to recover subaltern voices from official records, identifies Guha as a particularly effective practitioner and praises the specified essay. This is a methodological resource within a shared project, not generic mentorship or proof that mediated records provide unmediated speech.

edges.relationship: Spivak’s Can the Subaltern Speak supplies a later inflection and an unresolved representation problem in Chatterjee’s account of subalternity.
edges.evidence_note: Chatterjee describes Spivak’s one-woman case as introducing an individual, gender and race dimension absent from the early class-oriented project, then addresses the continuing problem of imposed legibility and speaking for others. The interviewer’s Morris/Butler vocabulary is not automatically attributed to him. This does not make Spivak founder of the early collective; no particular version of her essay is independently reread here.

edges.relationship: Foucault’s lectures on war, sovereignty and counter-history provide a framework Chatterjee extends to colonial state justification and the politics of scholarly knowledge.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2015 commentary calls the 1976 argument powerful, develops its law/war and counter-history account, then applies it to British colonial justification and knowledge/representation dilemmas. This is specified conceptual use with extensions and qualifications, not a universal formation claim. Quoted translated pages 37, 50, 98, 103, 134, 142 and 197 are Chatterjee’s references; the lecture edition and translation were not independently collated.

edges.relationship: Chatterjee suggests Foucault insufficiently emphasizes the transition from monarchical to popular sovereignty in accounts of modern disciplinary power.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2015 preliminary objection is explicitly tentative: Foucault may share responsibility for insufficient emphasis on a transition often missed in discussion. Chatterjee immediately quotes the second lecture to show that Foucault does state the relation. This is a narrow emphasis correction within sympathetic use, not a charge that Foucault wholly ignores popular sovereignty.

edges.relationship: Chatterjee endorses Trouillot’s suggestion that Haiti’s revolution produced an early postcolonial condition distinct from white-settler American revolutions.
edges.evidence_note: Direct 2012 answer, printed page 4, retains Chatterjee’s I think and Trouillot tried to suggest. The named argument supports his comparison of Haiti with white-settler revolutions; friendship alone does not establish the resource. No particular Trouillot book is identified or newly read, and the interview’s full Haitian chronology is not certified. This pair belongs to the Chatterjee dossier.

edges.relationship: Sarkar attributes a consequential application of Said’s colonial power-knowledge framework to Chatterjee’s Gandhi essay and Nationalist Thought.
edges.evidence_note: Sarkar (1997), 91, note 22, with context 90–92, identifies Chatterjee’s 1984 Gandhi essay and 1986 Nationalist Thought as points where Said’s colonial power-knowledge framework entered the project, and criticizes the resulting agency-erasing binary. This is explicit scholarly mediation by a critical former colleague, not fresh direct reading of those originals or acceptance of his verdict as settled. Said is not reduced to Foucault. Sarkar has no full endpoint; Orientalism remains unread by this review.

edges.relationship: Wood challenges Tuchman’s March of Folly for hindsight, anachronistic standards and overly narrow explanations, while praising parts of its narrative.
edges.evidence_note: The complete 1984 review reconstructs Tuchman’s contemporary-warning criteria before arguing that unpredictable outcomes make folly versus determination retrospectively unstable; Wood disputes the top-down Reformation and American Revolution accounts. He praises the Vietnam chapter while noting its thin account of opponents. This is Wood’s particular criticism, not a certified refutation, dismissal of all popular narrative, or repetition of Stone’s 1978 Mirror objection. Tuchman’s publisher opening explicitly requires contemporary recognition and alternatives; that intent remains alongside Wood’s objection.

sources.title: Richard McGrail interviews Partha Chatterjee on Subaltern Studies
sources.citation: Richard McGrail, “Subaltern Studies: A Conversation with Partha Chatterjee,” Cultural Anthropology, undated online transcript.

verification.note: Complete Q&A, official browser lines 27–72, was read and retained. Collective Gramsci reading, Spivak’s later inflection and Guha’s archive technique are Chatterjee’s testimony. Morris/Butler formulations in questions and the appended reading list are separate voices. The displayed page supplies no original date; a secondary association with 2012 is not an exact interview date. Local HTTP failed; the official browser witness supports the claims. Original Gramsci, Guha and Spivak texts were not newly read.

sources.title: Partha Chatterjee, Comments on Society Must Be Defended
sources.citation: Partha Chatterjee, “Comments on ‘Society Must Be Defended’,” Foucault 13/13, Columbia University, 24 November 2015.

verification.note: Complete signed commentary and three notes were checked through official browser lines 4–63. The retained browser witness contains the text; the local 403 response is challenge HTML, not the commentary. Bernard Harcourt is posting-account metadata, not the author. Chatterjee extends his reading of the 1976 lectures to colonial history and knowledge ethics; his emphasis objection is qualified. Quoted pagination is not an independently collated edition or translation. Original French lectures/books remain unread; the medical example is an attributed analytical hypothetical.

sources.title: Partha Chatterjee, Permanent Black interview
sources.citation: Permanent Black, “Great Kolkata Scholar interviewed,” 15 March 2011, interview with Partha Chatterjee.

verification.note: Complete Q1–Q5, following the separately attributed publisher introduction, were read. Repeated Gramsci reading, self-critical naming of political society, earlier nationalism books, Sanyal fieldwork, Marxist scholarship and tentative literary traces retain their different roles. The Columbia University Press excerpt of 21 December 2011 is a selective republication, not a second earlier interview. No Manifesto edition or full original Gramsci or other book reading is claimed.

sources.title: Barbara Tuchman, The March of Folly, publisher opening excerpt
sources.citation: Barbara W. Tuchman, The March of Folly: From Troy to Vietnam (first published 1984), publisher excerpt from the 1985 Random House Trade Paperbacks edition, ISBN 9780345308238, chapter 1 opening.

verification.note: Publisher opening read through the political-philosopher list, Oxenstierna and introduction of Rehoboam. Later excerpt paragraphs and the whole book remain unread. Contemporary recognition, feasible alternatives and collective policy are Tuchman’s stated criteria; they are not independent validation of historical examples. Unnamed historians are not assigned identities. Plato is a substantive but unattainable model; the wider philosopher list does not demonstrate work-specific formative debts. The 1985 edition is not the original publication date.

sources.title: Gordon S. Wood, History Lessons
sources.citation: Gordon S. Wood, “History Lessons,” New York Review of Books, 29 March 1984, review of Barbara W. Tuchman, The March of Folly.

verification.note: Complete review body checked at the original publication, with HTML/text retained. Wood praises narrative communication and the Vietnam chapter while criticizing didactic generalization, hindsight and elite explanations. Febvre and the 1973 Burke-edited collection are Wood’s resources, not Tuchman’s debts or a direct posthumous review. Quoted earlier Tuchman essays and the whole March of Folly remain unread; its publisher opening is separately checked. The article’s 1984 date is distinct from profile or footer dates; broad disciplinary diagnoses remain Wood’s judgments.

sources.title: E. A. Wrigley, The Quest for the Industrial Revolution
sources.citation: E. A. Wrigley, “The Quest for the Industrial Revolution,” Proceedings of the British Academy 121 (2003): 147–170; lecture delivered 12 November 2002.

verification.note: Actual 24-page publisher PDF. Selected 147–158 and 166–170, including relevant notes, were read; intervening 159–165 were not fully read. De Vries urban data and joint de Vries/van der Woude comparisons at 152–155, their qualifications at 157, and Mokyr’s calculation at 167–168/note 50 are explicit resources. No whole 2004 collection or original 1984, 1997 or 1993 works were read. Delivery, publication and reprint dates remain distinct; historical and numerical claims are not independently replicated.

cd_wrigley_ccc_1988.note: Actual 10-page publisher excerpt, locally OCRed: printed 1–8 reread, not all 9–10. The opening contrasts organic and mineral energy while retaining the bounded analytical strength of classical economists; definitions at 7–8 remain qualified. The 1987 lectures and altered 1988 book are distinguished. No whole-book or statistical verification claim; economic and ecological predictions remain the author’s.

ip_wrigley_energy_2010.note: Actual 10-page publisher excerpt: complete introduction 1–6 reread. Earlier selected 9–11 remain separately scoped, without a new whole-chapter claim. Institutional and scientific accounts at 4–5 are important, not rejected; environmental hazards and uncertain benefits at 1–2 qualify a purely beneficent portrait. Acknowledgments xiii were separately read. Numerical and historical claims remain unreplicated.

ip_wrigley_reconstitution_1997.note: Actual scanned 10-page publisher excerpt, locally OCRed: printed 3–4 and opening 5 reread. Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield retain joint authorship. Note 1 says Henry perfected the technique but acknowledges Edin (1915) and Hyrenius (1942); the Crulai study is joint Gautier/Henry work. Vann and Eversley are further resources. Originals, registers and statistics remain unchecked; no sole-invention or sole-authorship claim.

ip_wrigley_schofield_1981.note: Actual 30-page 1989 front matter, downloaded and OCRed: new Introductory Note xiii–xv and related-publication list xxxi–xxxiii read. Wrigley and Schofield retain joint authorship, with Lee and Oeppen contributions. This is not the original 1981 preface at xxxv onward, which the excerpt omits, or a whole 1989 preface reading. The reply to Lindert allows improvements while contesting age, census and fertility assumptions; no adjudication or original Lindert/Lee/Lam reading. Earlier selected introduction 1–5 remains scoped. A listed Mokyr review is metadata only.

cd_berg_hudson_1990.note: Actual 62-page May 1990 working paper: selected 1–4 and 20–21, plus the complete Demography section 30–33, read. Earlier selected 1–6, 38–39 and notes 1, 5–6 remain separately scoped. Joint Berg/Hudson criticism targets Wrigley/Schofield aggregate causation and male-labour productivity, retaining regional, class and sector variation, mortality, nuptiality and Schofield’s own revision. Original tables and Levine/Goldstone empirical studies remain unread and unreplicated. The preliminary 1990 paper is not silently treated as the 1992 article.

genovese.note: Reread the retained licensed Everand preview from the Higham research, whose canonical URL matches this source; frozen Higham files are unchanged. A new request timed out, so no new successful download is claimed. Complete August 1973 preface and acknowledgments, title/permissions, opening paternalism and selected Farmers, Planters, and Overseers paragraphs were checked; not the whole preview/book. Original 1974, Vintage 1976 and ebook 2011 manifestations remain distinct. Woodward’s framing, Davis’s ideas/revisions, Rawick’s teaching, joint Engerman/Fogel work and Elizabeth Fox-Genovese’s rewriting retain their different roles. Du Bois receives only qualified support; demographics and the exact underlying Du Bois work are not independently verified. No new direct Gramsci reading.

johnson_genovese_review.note: Complete original July 2001 review read through its final day-to-day-resistance paragraph and issue 1.4 notice; recommendation cards excluded. Praise for durable categories coexists with criticism of paternalism, terror, sale, coercion and revolutionary aspirations; a simplistic denial-of-agency caricature is expressly rejected. Existing edge_1609 and edge_1610 already record this debate and Gramsci mediation, so no duplicate or fresh original-Gramsci reading is inferred. Historical examples are not independently audited.

rh188_chatterjee_interview.note: Complete original 11-page 2012 article checked through the Cambridge-hosted DOI 10.1017/S1557466012033256. Its APJJF publication of 8 October 2012, Humanity dialogue origin and added APJJF afterword remain distinct. Initial APJJF 403 is not article text. Earlier 2–3 is reinforced; page 4 supplies Trouillot’s Haiti argument, 6 Bentham, 7 the Schmitt distinction, 8 Perry Anderson criticism, 9 Polanyi, and 10–11 the speculative afterword. The Black Hole book and cited originals remain unread. Page 4 was visually checked. Platform migration dates do not replace publication.

chatterjee_fragments.note: Institutional UNAM seven-page scan contains title and chapter 1, printed 3–13, not the whole book or preface. OCR and rendered pages support selected 4–7: praise of Anderson precedes the modularity objection, and print-capitalism is accepted with qualifications. Pages 9 and 12–13 concern new patriarchy and mutually conditioned elite/subaltern domains; no absolute division or second Anderson pair/kind is added. The Princeton 1993 manifestation is not conflated with Sarkar’s Delhi 1994 citation.

sarkar_decline.note: Selected 82–85, 87–92 and 95–98 read from the NAU single-chapter teaching scan of Writing Social History (1997), 82–108; not the entire chapter. The course electronic-reserve list confirms this is the assigned single chapter. Printed 90–91 were visually checked. Page 91/note 22 attributes Said’s framework through Chatterjee’s 1984 essay and 1986 book while criticizing binary homogenization and erased agency. Page 92 concerns elite figures and caste/class/gender neglect; praise at 95 coexists with objections at 96–98 to material/spiritual division, exclusions and community valorization. Sarkar’s judgment is attributed, not settled. Those Chatterjee originals remain unread; Sarkar lacks a full endpoint.

w3_guha_chibber_verso_2014.note: Official Verso response of 25 February 2014 downloaded. Selected numbered paragraphs 6–9, 30–40 and 49–53 plus notes were checked, not the entire response. Petitjean’s introduction is separate from Chibber’s voice. Criticism addresses abstract labour, difference, purported ironic nationalism and nonengagement; Guha passages also concern Chatterjee’s defense. Chatterjee’s original 2013 EPW article remains unavailable, so its positions are Chibber-reported. Kafila embeds a debate with Nigam commentary, not a transcript; neither video nor comments were used as Chatterjee testimony. Existing Guha group route and mediation remain; Chibber lacks an endpoint.

tuchman_search_excerpt.note: Complete publisher-provided In Search of History excerpt reread, from childhood fiction through the Guns of August weather example; not the entire Practicing History or necessarily the full original lecture. Childhood authors, Babbitt/Lowes/McIlwain courses, the explicitly most formative Widener stacks, Bowen’s reader-turn principle, Macaulay’s formula and qualified Ranke ideal retain their different roles. Emerson/Poe and Pascal are aesthetic/craft examples; Scott/Comines are nested inside the Ranke quotation. Originals were not collated. Existing edge_552 remains; publisher 1982 edition metadata does not newly establish the lecture date.

stone_tuchman_review.note: Official 1978 HTML retained. Selected opening analogy/professional criteria and later merits/explanation passages reread; this does not claim a second whole-body reading. Froissart, Veblen and Geertz are Stone’s interventions, not their direct criticism or Tuchman’s debts. Praise of evidence, restraint and writing coexists with institutional, bourgeois, peasant and explanatory objections. Prior complete-reading scope and edge_554 remain; historical generalizations and forecasts stay attributed.

fox_stone_tuchman_exchange.note: Complete original Fox-Genovese letter and Stone reply reread. Elizabeth challenges status-based dismissal, progress/capitalism assumptions and absent professional disagreement, while defending social groups/material dislocation and expressly denying that Tuchman subscribes to Marxism. Miskimin is her counterexample, not Tuchman’s demonstrated debt. Stone distinguishes research from haute vulgarisation, praises scholarly/prose virtues, qualifies the disaster narrative and invokes Carr as professional reading. Eugene’s books are an analogy, not evidence he authored Elizabeth’s letter. This is reception of a completed 1978 book, not prior influence.

rationale: Existing endpoints only; preserve named mediation, coauthorship, critical qualifications, edition and reading limits. All old graph records unchanged apart from append-only source reading notes. Tocqueville excluded as an owned dossier or newly read primary body, not as an existing resource endpoint in another historian’s own testimony. No new biographies, fields, life facts, chronology or dissertation analysis. OpenAlex remains paused.
